To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“In the case when all measurements are done using the same measurement instrument – or, at least, using a limited number of measurement instruments – the variance of interval measurements can be computed in polynomial time.”
in general statistical analysis of interval measurement data is an NP-Hard problem, but there are several cases in which a feasible algorithm is possible.

(i) the statistical analysis of interval (i.e., imprecise) data is in general NP-hard, (ii) there is at least one case in which a polynomial-time algorithm exists, (iii) we have found several new cases where feasible algorithms exist, and (iv) we have proved that there is no feasible algorithm for the general case.
In summary, our research is concerned with
finding the minimal number of measurements that are needed to compute the variance of an interval data set.

developing new algorithms for the following problems: 1. computing the sample mean and the sample variance of interval data 2. computing the sample median of interval data 3. computing the quantiles of interval data 4. computing the sample covariance matrix of interval data.
the development of new algorithms for the analysis of statistical data, in which the measurements are done with a certain degree of inaccuracy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
statistical analysis of interval measurements is feasible in many practical situations.
the statistical analysis of interval measurement data is an NP-complete problem, but there are several cases in which the statistical analysis of such data is a feasible problem.
the statistical analysis of interval measurements is an NP-hard computational problem, but in many practically important cases, there are feasible algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in general, statistical inference for interval data is an intractable problem.
, for a wide range of cases, we can now compute the variance of an interval data set in a polynomial time.

, in the case when the number of different measuring instrument is bounded by some fixed constant (e.g., 3 or 5), then it is possible to compute the variance of the interval data, and to solve several other important problems for statistical analysis of interval (or more general, fuzzy) data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for some cases, the NP-hardness of statistical analysis of interval measurement data is a consequence of the complexity of the measurement process, not the complexity of the statistical analysis.
in some cases, statistical analysis of the interval data is feasible.
in many cases, statistical analysis of real-world data can be done in polynomial time.
